#1482. Russell must do something wacky now after disappointing Bahrain GP qualifying

Never mind the lack of an ice vest, George Russell is somehow going to need to be the coolest man in Malaysia if he is to turn seventh on the grid into a positive result in Sunday’s Bahrain Grand Prix.The first race in Sepang in nearly a decade – a late addition to the calendar because of the conflict in the Middle East – promises to be an absolute scorcher. It might even be worth setting your alarm for the 8am UK start time. Red Bull’s Max Verstappen will start in pole position for the first time this year. He will have Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton alongside him.

It will be the first time since Hungary 2023 that those two gladiators have started on a front row together. Throw in sweltering temperatures, low grip, high tyre degradation, and the ever-present threat of a Malaysian monsoon sweeping through Sepang, and you have the potential for fireworks.

Russell might need something wacky if he is to do anything from that far back. This was a desperately disappointing result for the British driver. After his victory in Baku last weekend, Russell was hopeful he had finally found the winning formula and that he could continue to take the fight to his team-mate Kimi Antonelli, whom he trails in the drivers’ championship by 66pts.

Eighth, four places behind, and 0.24sec slower than the Italian, was not what Russell would have had in mind, although both Mercedes drivers will rise a spot because of the five-place grid penalty meted out to Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar for exceeding his engine allowance for the season.Russell will have felt particularly disappointed as Antonelli only got one run in Q3 after using up a set of soft tyres when he made a mistake and went off track in Q2. He now trails his team mate nine-seven in qualifying head-to-head this year.“No to be honest,” Russell admitted when asked whether he knew why he was so slow. “This circuit is an outlier in terms of the abrasiveness of the tarmac.“The lap times seven years ago were six or seven seconds faster and at certain points on the track it feels like you are driving on gravel, which is the same for everyone, but it is clearly affecting us more than others.”Mercedes’ lack of performance was doubly unexpected because not only did they arrive here with a massive upgrade package, but Russell revealed this week that he and Antonelli were foregoing the cooling vests you see some drivers sporting on the grid, in favour of car performance.

Toto Wolff, the Mercedes team principal, admitted it was a head-scratcher. “Very difficult to understand,” the Austrian said. “We have been a little bit caught out on Friday with some car behaviour that we did not see all year, but then you can say it is very hot and the tarmac is different to all the [other] tracks. It looked really good this morning. We seemed to have, at least with Kimi, made a step in understanding. And then, qualifying was a little bit back to what we saw before, just no performance.”

Still, both titles are in the bag so Wolff cannot be too unhappy. Russell is the one who will be really miffed. He really needs to be beating his team-mate pretty much every race weekend if he is to get his title hopes back on track.

At the front, the mood was somewhat different. Verstappen became the first non-Mercedes-powered pilot to take a pole position this year. It was a first pole position for Red Bull Powertrains, too. And with his long run pace looking more than decent, Verstappen should really hold on for his first win of 2026. Hamilton will do his best to hang on to the Dutchman’s coattails. The seven-time champion was delighted when told he had taken P2. “Let’s go guys! Finally! Great job guys, really great job. Car felt great.”

This was indeed an excellent performance from the Ferrari man – and just the tonic for the Scuderia after weeks of gossip and speculation. Hamilton was admittedly three tenths slower than his rival, which he put purely down to a power deficit on the straights, but he said he was hopeful his long run pace was more competitive. The last time a F1 held a race was held here back in 2017, the British driver claimed pole only to be overhauled by a youthful Verstappen. He will be desperate to turn the tables this time.

“It was really hard to find a good balance, and we made one change before qualifying and we hit the sweet spot,” he reflected afterwards. “I am so, so grateful. I will try my best to hold on to Max tomorrow, and if we are in the fight that would be awesome. I’ve been talking too much, but I guess you talk more when you are happy. It was my best lap of the year. It feels like I won, and I will give it everything tomorrow.”

It is Russell, though, who needs a result even more badly if he is to remain a factor in the championship. “As a team, we have yet to have a bad race this whole season and this was clearly a very bad qualifying for us,” he admitted, adding that “all the numbers” from the upgrade package suggested it was an improvement on the old car. “But I think there is going to be a lot happening tomorrow. The tyre deg is huge and race pace will be king. So even though today was a real disappointment it is not the be all and end all.”

No. 1 ☝️#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/01PqrckQS9

Tomorrow’s race will be the first time since Hungary 2023 that Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton will start on the front row together. It is a reasonable run down to turn one and there are overtaking opportunities through the first few corners at Sepang, with it being similar to the configuration in China, with plenty of lines and moves on offer.

Respect between two great champions 🤩#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/fbZ6aoKRyw

“Very difficult to understand. We have been a little bit caught out on Friday with some car behaviour that we did not see all year, but then you can say it is very hot and the tarmac is the different to all the (other) tracks. It looked really good this morning. We seemed to have, at least with Kimi [Antonelli], made a step in understanding. And then, qualifying was a little bit back to what we saw before, just no performance.”

On Kimi Antonelli’s track limits breach in Q2:

“Not good, because Q2 you know you are going to get through. You lose a set [of softs] in a qualifying that is so tight, where we are on the back foot. That is not good.”

Lewis Hamilton says this is the biggest crowd he has ever seen at Sepang, thanking the fans for making it here today. That is actually a bigger compliment than many watching at home may realise. The traffic this weekend has been horrendous. After 10 years without a race in Malaysia, during which time F1 has grown massively, I think they have forgotten how to do traffic management. Shuttles are inconsistent, taxis can’t get in/out, it’s taking forever just to reach the airport a few kilometres away - some fans have been braving the heat and walking. It took over two hours to get back into Kuala Lumpur last night (48km). My understanding is the Bahrainis are organising the race this year, while local forces are handling the traffic outside the circuit.

“The car has been very good since last week. It is good to come back [from his wrist injury] at such a time and I am enjoying it, fighting for the top three. Even though it was not my finest qualifying session it is a good feeling.

“It is a bit unfortunate we take a penalty on a track where we are that fast but, from eighth, I am confident we can come through the field and come back for a good result.”

“I love this energy [from the crowd]. Big, big thank you to Malaysia for welcoming us. It is so hot here. I keep saying it, but that has made it a massive challenge for the tyres, the car, the mechanics in the garage. I am really, really thankful to my team. We made so many changes through all these practice sessions. Because the cars are sliding, the tyres are overheating, it was really hard to find a good balance, and we made one last change going into qualifying and I think we hit the sweet spot. To be able to close the gap to two or three tenths to Max [Verstappen], who has been so quick all weekend, is great, and I am so grateful.

“I am much happier with where the car is, but tomorrow is a completely different ballgame. Making these tyres last around this track, they are overheating from the get-go. Every little bit of wheelspin you have, every little snap you have makes a difference of how far you are going to go. I like to think we have got a good balance. Max was really quick on his long runs, so I will just try my best to hold onto him tomorrow.”

A reminder that Isack Hadjar will drop from third to eighth after his grid penalty.

QUALIFYING CLASSIFICATIONCan't wait for Sunday! 🤩#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/qqi8hPDcKA

“It is fantastic. We have been trying many grand prix to get pole. Sometimes a bit closer than others but to finally get it, from where we started the season, pretty incredible. I am happy with today and, for sure, I am going to try and win tomorrow. When you start first, that is the target.”

Big disappointment that for Russell. After his win in Baku, where he said he finally felt hooked up to the car, he was desperate to build the momentum. P8, four places behind Antonelli, was not what he would have had in mind. Has it all to do in the race tomorrow.

Excellent (though not unexpected) pole for Verstappen, and a very good P2 for Hamilton. Could be some fireworks on the front row tomorrow.

*Hadjar’s three-place grid penalty will drop him down to eighth place for the race tomorrow.

Neither of the Red Bulls can improve in the first sector but it is those behind them who need significant improvements. The two Ferraris are going along nicely at the start of their final flying laps. Hadjar is unable to improve despite a purple final sector. Verstappen then goes fastest in the final sector and improves his advantage at the top.

Hamilton meanwhile went fastest in the middle sector and goes second fastest overall. Piastri cannot improve but stays ahead of Russell.

Norris is the final man across the line but is only fast enough for P6. That means that Verstappen takes pole in Malaysia, which is the first time this season that Red Bull have taken pole position. Hamilton is second with Hadjar third, although the Frenchman has a five-place grid penalty.

MAX VERSTAPPEN TAKES POLE FOR THE BAHRAIN GRAND PRIX IN MALAYSIA!! 👊#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/NgtaCAZacL

The two Red Bulls, who are one and two at the moment, will be the first two drivers across the line on these final efforts.

The other nine drivers in Q3 are in the pits so young Antonelli has the track to himself as he sets his one and only flying lap of Q3. He is over four tenths down on Verstappen through the first sector and has plenty of work to do.

The championship leader sets a decent middle sector where he loses no more time to Verstappen. As it stands he would put himself third before the others do their final runs. He comes across the line in P3 but will have the likes of Hamilton, Piastri, Leclerc, Norris and Russell trying to surpass him.

Russell is the first across the line and sets a time of a 1:36.032. He does not last long at the top as he is immediately displaced by Hadjar, who is half a second quicker.

Hamilton then comes over the line in second, just ahead of his teammate Leclerc. Piastri puts himself between the two Ferraris.

What about Verstappen? The man who won here the last time we were in Malaysia continues his great form today and goes quickest by more than three tenths.

Antonelli now heads out and will have the track to himself really. This is going to be the championship leader’s only flying lap of Q3.

Russell is the first man to head out for his first flying lap in Q3. Antonelli has remained in the pits with just one new set of softs remaining. Verstappen, who right now feels like the favourite for pole, will be one of the last across the line in these first attempts of Q3.

The fight for pole position in Sepang begins now as the green light is on at the end of the pit lane to get Q3 going.

Antonelli, due to that lap time deletion in Q2, has just one new set of softs for Q3, which could prove costly in his attempts to try and take pole.

P12 the best qualifying result of the season for Alonso. It was only his second time in Q2 after Hungary (P16).

I should add, P14 was also Lance Stroll’s best qualifying result of the season. His first outing in Q2 this year.

11. Liam Lawson (Racing Bulls)12. Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin)13. Carlos Sainz (Williams)14. Lance Stroll (Aston Martin)15. Franco Colapinto (Alpine)16. Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls)

With grid penalties already on their way, neither Colapinto nor Lindblad set lap times in Q2.

Verstappen, Leclerc, Piastri, Norris, Hadjar and Russell all remain in the pits. A bit of a risk for Russell down in eighth but his time should be enough to get into Q3.

Lindblad, who will start tomorrow’s race at the back of the grid after penalties, gives his teammate Lawson a tow down the back straight and it works as Lawson just sneaks into the top ten.

Can Bortoleto get back ahead though of Lawson? Yes he can and he will take the final place in Q3. Lawson thought he might be through but the tow was not enough.

Lindblad, who's taking a grid penalty for Sunday's race, gave team mate Lawson a tow but it wasn't quite enough to send the Kiwi into Q3#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/IMlrqg4ENv

As the young Italian starts his flying lap, there is no-one else out on track so no traffic. He is a lot more cautious at turn six this time than last time, when he had his lap time deleted.

He has not set blistering first and second sector times but a purple final sector puts him into second and the Italian is safely into Q3.

Plenty of other drivers are now heading around the track for their final flying laps of Q2.

11. Lance Stroll (Aston Martin)12. Carlos Sainz (Williams)13. Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes)14. Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls)15. Franco Colapinto (Alpine)16. Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin)

Mercedes have put a brand new set of softs onto Antonelli’s car as he heads out promptly, with no lap time to his name so far. Antonelli is still disputing the lap deletion over team radio but his team tell him the images show he exceeded track limits. This is now a lot of pressure on the championship leader; any mistake now and he will not make Q3. His teammate Russell is only in seventh.

Antonelli was fourth fastest but has had his lap time deleted for exceeding track limits at turn six. That is a big moment in Q2 and could prove problematic if he gets into Q3. Antonelli appeared to be confused when he was told about his lap deletion over team radio but the on-board view looked pretty clear-cut.

Piastri then comes across the line in third.

Here's the moment Kimi ran wide 👀#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/E0VdWdBt8x

The Dutchman looks in a great spot at the moment to take pole position today and his 1:35.696 is very quick. He is nearly four tenths quicker than Antonelli.

How about the Ferraris? Leclerc was quickest in the middle sector but is nearly three tenths down on Verstappen. Hamilton puts himself into third place. Russell is more than half a second down on Verstappen.

Verstappen has been shown a black and white flag for driving unnecessarily slowly. I doubt he will get a grid penalty for that but it will be a warning for the Dutchman.

Anyway, the drivers, other than Colapinto and Alonso, are on flying laps, with Verstappen currently fastest inthe first sector.

The green light is showing at the end of the pit lane and the second part of qualifying is under way. Like the start of Q1, it is hardly a stampede to go out.

17. Nico Hulkenberg (Audi)18. Oliver Bearman (Haas)19. Esteban Ocon (Haas)20. Alex Albon (Williams)21. Valtteri Bottas (Cadillac)22. Sergio Perez (Cadillac)

The Aston Martin of Stroll improves significantly from 20th and is set to make Q2, as is his teammate Alonso. A bit of a surprise to see the Aston Martins improve and make it into Q2.

Go Fernando! 🤩 Go Lance! 🤩First double Q2 appearance this season 🙌#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/xjiWYv6ycr

That has seen the Audi of Hulkenberg drop into the drop zone and the German is out. For contrast, his teammate improves to go into eighth place! Hulkenberg had a big lock up into turn 14, which proved very costly.

As it stands, eight of the top nine are remaining in the garage. Russell is in ninth and has not gone out but Gasly above him in eighth has. You would imagine Russell is perfectly safe.

17. Esteban Ocon (Haas)18. Alex Albon (Williams)19. Oliver Bearman (Haas)20. Lance Stroll (Aston Martin)21. Valtteri Bottas (Cadillac)22. Sergio Perez (Cadillac)

Ocon, in 17th, is quite far off Hulkenberg in 16th and needs more than four tenths to usurp him.

The screens in the media centre here in Sepang tell me that the air temp right now is 32.8C and the track temp is 58C. It feels even hotter. Lots of chat about cooling vests this week, which are optional. George Russell is among the drivers who isn’t using one, which is interesting a) because Russell has suffered badly from heat in the past (Qatar, Singapore) and b) because he says Mercedes chose to put the development money into car upgrades instead.

It’s an interesting admission. Not everyone is sold on the idea of cooling vests. Ferrari and McLaren will definitely be using them this weekend, for instance. Max Verstappen won’t as he doesn’t like them. Russell thinks the FIA should just develop the tech themselves and it shouldn’t be part of the budget cap.

“Our team have put a lot of emphasis this year on the cockpit temperature,” he said. “We won’t be running the cooling vest because we haven’t put the resource into making it robust enough. I feel we need the FIA just to step in and say ‘Here’s some money extra in the cost cap or there’s an external company who’s going to develop it for everybody’. Because we should all be wearing it. When it works, it works great. So, I would like to wear it this week, and I would like to wear it next week. But the team asked me...look, we can develop it, and we can put the money towards it...[but at a cost].

He added: “The top itself is not expensive ..you’ve got to effectively make a system where you can fit a block of dry ice or actual ice, and then has the airflow to circulate the cool water throughout. If that system isn’t robust enough, then suddenly you have no circulation, and then you get hot. You get ambient temperature circulating. The vest is one-design, but the system that circulates the water is different [at different teams].”

The two Ferraris are on medium tyres but Leclerc still puts himself into second place. He is then displaced by Hamilton, who slots in behind Verstappen. Good times from the Ferraris on the mediums.

What about the McLarens? Norris goes sixth fastest but is more than six tenths down on Verstappen. Then comes Piastri, who goes fourth fastest, just under four tenths off Verstappen.

Arguably the three favourites for pole; Antonelli, Russell and Verstappen, are all on flying laps.

The first sector goes the way of Verstappen, who is purple, and then the Dutchman goes purple in the middle sector.

Antonelli is two tenths faster than his teammate Russell but Verstappen is over half a second quicker than the Mercedes. Hadjar is then second fastest to show the pace in the Red Bull this weekend.

Most of the teams waited and waited to come out and then suddenly lots of drivers are sent out, resulting in a queue in the pits! With the high track temperatures and high degradation, the drivers are crawling around on their out laps to preserve these soft tyres.

Bumper to bumper in the pit lane! #F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/ff8JO9kB1g

The two Haas drivers have a free track to themselves whilst everyone else bides their time. In theory, as the hour of qualifying goes on, the track temperature should decrease and the more rubber that is laid down the faster the track should get.

Finally, just before the two Haas drivers finish their first flying laps, the rest of the grid is starting to emerge, led by the Mercedes duo.

The green light is showing at the end of the pit lane and Q1 is officially under way. The two Haas drivers are the first to head out. Other than that, it is a quiet start to Q1.

The top four teams; Mercedes, Red Bull, Ferrari and McLaren, all have a genuine chance of taking pole in Sepang today. I think the true favourites though have to be the Mercedes duo and Max Verstappen but with how close it between all four of the teams you cannot rule anything out.

It is 33 degrees celsius air temperature, with the track temperature up at 58 degrees.

Not long to wait now until qualifying begins. It is hot, humid and dry in Sepang right now. As we know in Malaysia, the weather can change quickly and thunderstorms can roll in quite quickly but it looks like today’s qualifying will be a dry one. This will be one of if not the hottest qualifying sessions of the season, so much so that we are seeing umbrellas going up to get some shade from the sun rather than sheltering from any rain.

This will be important to consider after qualifying finishes as there will be some shuffling around:

Isack Hadjar (Red Bull): five-place grid penalty- new internal combustion engineFranco Colapinto (Alpine): ten-place grid penalty- new engineFranco Colapinto (Alpine): five-place grid penalty- causing a collision in BakuArvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls): back of the grid- complete power unit change

Hadjar has looked good since returning from his wrist injury so could be fighting it out near the front of the grid, although his five-place penalty will drop him down. We know Lindblad will be at the back and is very likely to be joined there by Colapinto, who is not going to be qualifying high up in the top ten in his Alpine.

Haas have announced that Frenchman Esteban Ocon will leave at the end of this season. Ocon now faces an uncertain future, with it difficult to see a spot for him on the F1 grid next season. There are suggestions that the 30-year-old’s replacement will be Brazilian Ferrari junior Rafael Camara, although nothing has been confirmed on that front. 21-year-old Camara currently leads the Formula 2 championship.

TGR Haas F1 Team and Esteban Ocon will part ways at the conclusion of the 2026 season. With plenty of racing ahead, our focus remains on working together to maximize every opportunity through to the final race of the year.#HaasF1 #F1 pic.twitter.com/4iQAuqnSyA

Aston Martin have now confirmed their driver line-up for next season, retaining both Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll. There had been reports that Alonso had been contemplating retirement but the 45-year-old will continue into another season.

Aston Martin Aramco confirms Lance and Fernando will continue as the team's drivers in 2027. Read more: ​https://t.co/ePyjJdyAIB pic.twitter.com/VogFUEbNxy

Other than the second seat alongside Ollie Bearman at Haas, the only other team to keep an eye on is Racing Bulls, with no definite confirmation on their exact driver line-up for next season.

Ferrari this week have publicly backed their team principal Frederic Vasseur, amid speculation over the Frenchman’s position and comments made by former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner, who said the job at Ferrari would be a “dream job”. Ferrari, who sit second in the constructors’ standings, have not won the drivers’ championship since 2007 (Kimi Raikkonen) and the constructors’ since 2008. Here is a snippet from Tom Cary’s piece on the matter:

In a hastily convened media call on Tuesday morning, Maria Conti, Ferrari’s chief communication officer, said the Scuderia had decided to issue a vote of confidence in Vasseur in response “not just to the story of Mr Horner, but in general, the speculation about Fred”.

“Ferrari has made its choices,” Conti said. “We have confidence – full confidence – in Fred Vasseur and in his team, and we continue to do so.

“At this time, it’s really important that the team remains united and cohesive, and we are focused with all the energy on the work ahead.”

“It is great to be back [in Malaysia]. I am really enjoying the track. We have had some wonderful races here over time. It is actually the 20th time we have been here, it started in 1999, and it is really exciting to be back. I really enjoyed getting out on the track and watching the cars closely.

“The drivers are super fit and they have some cooling but it is not easy. But you almost cannot get enough fluid through your body before your stomach gives up. Having this race and Singapore back-to-back increases that challenge.”

Especially with the big upgrade they have brought this weekend, Mercedes’ lead at the summit is looking unassailable right now.

Almost nine years ago to the day, Max Verstappen took just his second race victory in Formula 1. Lewis Hamilton, who took pole position, and Daniel Ricciardo joined Verstappen on the podium. Despite being nine years ago, plenty of drivers still on the grid were racing that weekend. Here they are and who they were racing for:

Max Verstappen (Red Bull) Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes) Valtteri Bottas (Mercedes) Esteban Ocon (Force India)Nico Hulkenberg (Renault)Sergio Perez (Force India)Fernando Alonso (McLaren)Lance Stroll (Williams)Carlos Sainz (Toro Rosso)Pierre Gasly (Toro Rosso)

With Russell winning in Baku and Antonelli finishing fifth, the latter’s championship lead was cut to 66 points. If Russell is going to usurp his teammate, he is going to need a few more similar results to last weekend due to the size of Antonelli’s lead. If Antonelli were to suffer a retirement, then that completely changes the outlook.

Formula One returns to Malaysia for round 16 of the season for the Bahrain Grand Prix. That probably sounds strange but after the Bahrain Grand Prix was originally postponed in March, F1 reinstated it to the calendar with Malaysia hosting it because of the ongoing war in the Middle East. Despite being held in Malaysia, Bahrain have retained the naming rights for the event, which is officially known as the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. The last time Formula One was in Malaysia was nine years ago back in 2017, when a young whippersnapper named Max Verstappen, still four years away from winning his first world championship, claimed just his second victory.

Last time out around the streets of Baku, Mercedes’ George Russell claimed victory at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, pipping Verstappen by just a tenth of a second. That was Russell’s first grand prix win since June and cuts his team-mate Kimi Antonelli’s lead in the drivers’ standings to 66 points. Antonelli had a challenging weekend in Baku, starting 16th after a crash in qualifying and coming home in fifth to see his championship lead to Russell cut by 15 points.

Verstappen was quickest in first practice yesterday, with the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc fastest in second practice. Earlier today, championship leader Antonelli was nearly three tenths clear of the field in third practice. Mercedes, 160 points clear at the top of the constructors’ standings, have brought significant upgrades this weekend, which includes a new floor, rear suspension and rear corner. It is the team’s first significant car update since the Canadian Grand at the end of May.

This race in Malaysia represents the second leg of the season’s first flyaway triple header, with the Singapore Grand Prix to come next weekend, so the demands on the teams and the drivers are incredibly high. Qualifying from Sepang gets under way at 9am (GMT).

#1481. Nani, Man Utd, and the unfair portrayal of a ‘frustrating’ talent

Throughout the majority of his playing career, former Manchester United winger Nani has been called ‘frustrating’. Why not just enjoy the show?

Life can be frustrating. Hangnails. Queues. Taxes. These things aren’t the end of the world, but all of them, despite their smallness, can frustrate.

In an interview with Ball Street in 2017, former Manchester United and England defender Rio Ferdinand got some personal frustration off his chest, talking about one particular bugbear from his time at Old Trafford.

“I think the most frustrating thing,” he said, “is when you know you’ve got players in your team with undoubted ability — great ability, got everything — but don’t consistently get that out onto the pitch.”

The object of that frustration was Nani, a team-mate of Ferdinand’s for seven years.

According to Ferdinand, Nani simply never learned to control his talents. What happened in training, mesmerising skills and thumping shots, was only occasionally replicated on match-day, and the winger, for the most part, simply didn’t live up to his potential.

Ferdinand wasn’t alone in holding this opinion. A cursory search for ‘frustrating Nani’ brings up countless results, with everybody from football journalists to other ex-United players chiming in with similar words.

Nani has to be one of the most frustrating players around. So much natural ability but you just don't know what your going to get from him

— Danny Higginbotham (@Higginbotham05) June 16, 2014

https://twitter.com/grahamruthven/status/741671670453264384

Also a big evening for nani playing against Chelsea. Such a frustrating player. Immense ability but so inconsistent.

— Danny Higginbotham (@Higginbotham05) September 30, 2014

In what was probably the most extreme case of Nani frustration, former United academy player Danny Higginbotham actually came to the same conclusion twice in the space of three months.

The frustrated have some justification for their annoyance. Nani’s talent was – and still is – evident, but during his spell in England, people saw that talent as being regularly misused — expended on needless tricks, ambitious long-range shots and generally poor decision making.

That ability to frustrate was increased by a frequent proximity to Cristiano Ronaldo, a player who would prove impossible to replace at Mancheter United and who, funnily enough, once got incredibly frustrated with his younger compatriot.

When Nani ruined one of Ronaldo's greatest goals for Portugal 😂 pic.twitter.com/aUPE4bzu5I

— Mark O'Haire (@MarkOHaire) April 15, 2020

For three specific reasons, however, I believe it is impossible for a football fan to consider Nani a frustration, a disappointment or anything less than the genius that he is.

When Manchester United and Chelsea contested the 2008 Champions League Final, the match went to a penalty shootout.

After eight kicks, and with Cristiano Ronaldo’s miss separating the scores, the spotlight turned to the teams’ respective fifth-in-line takers. The deciders. The key men.

For United, the responsibility was handed to 21-year-old Nani, playing in the final match of his debut season; for Chelsea, it was 27-year-old captain John Terry.

For Nani’s side to have any chance of winning the game, the young winger needed to score and hope that Terry did not.

The coincidental pairing of Nani and Terry back in 2008 is interesting, because if anybody knows what ‘frustration’ is, it’s surely the man who has just fallen on his arse in front of 70,000 people at the most important moment of his career.

For the fans, too: if seeing a player on your team attempt one too many step-overs can be frustrating, then seeing your captain — an ostensibly non-frustrating player — fail where the chief frustrater has just calmly succeeded must be the epitome of frustration.

Less than a year into his Manchester United career, Nani stepped up ahead of senior players like Ryan Giggs and — appropriately — Rio Ferdinand, converting a critical penalty against a world-class goalkeeper.

For that, he earned the right to attempt an infinite number of step-overs.

﻿

Nani has defied his critics on several other occasions.

In February 2008, a few months before that penalty against Chelsea, the winger provided some curious quotes to the Daily Mail.

“In Portugal I have done this many times, but it is only because it is an entertaining spectacle and not because I disrespect my rivals,” he said.

“I am a professional and am always very respectful with all the opposing players, but I do appreciate now that it may have looked bad.”

In truth, what Nani had just done — the grave action for which he was publicly apologising — actually looked pretty good.

With Manchester United 4-0 up in an FA Cup tie against Arsenal, the Portuguese attacker pulled off a frankly hilarious series of keep-ups — knee, head, head, head, knee, knee, foot — to shield the ball from a furious (and, in all honesty, frustrated) William Gallas.

“Professionals don’t like that, when players turn on a bit of circus stuff,” explained John Motson just seconds after chuckling at the events unfolding in front of him.

﻿

Nani’s infamous seal dribble may not have won his team the FA Cup, but it was anything but frustrating.

Frustration is having to get up at 6am, catch the bus and work a rubbish job. Football, as Nani well knows, should be a release from that frustration.

If John Terry and William Gallas falling over for various reasons isn’t enough to convince fans of Nani’s value, then perhaps the winger’s trophies are.

The most important of the bunch came two years ago, when the former Man United player took the captain’s armband from the injured Cristiano Ronaldo — the player he was, in the eyes of many demanding observers, supposed to emulate — in the final of Euro 2016.

Charged with the responsibility of leading his team, Nani helped Portugal to their first ever European Championship.

“It was a very strange feeling when Cristiano went off because I was very upset about losing our captain and our best player,” Nani told The Guardian a month after the tournament.

“But very quickly I had to put my head up and try to help the team, try to give them the confidence and motivation to continue. I had to do my job. I had to do what captains have to do.”

The final at the Stade de France was frustrating — agonising, even — for the injured Ronaldo.

For the deputy captain, however, it was simply a matter of doing what he did best: dribble, cross, dribble, cross.

Many fans (and former team-mates) will still view Nani as one of the Premier League’s most frustrating players, but considering all the entertainment the player has provided over the years — the long-range screamers, the seal dribble, the backflip celebration — as well as the significant achievements that have accompanied those moments, you have to wonder if that frustration could be cured by just… lightening up a little.

Football, as Nani has shown, can be fun. Let it be.

#1479. Would Wayne Rooney have worked in Pep Guardiola’s Barcelona?

“I would have loved to play for Barcelona,” Wayne Rooney said recently.

“Barça beat us in the Champions League final and they didn’t have a reference No. 9. I think it would have been easy to play in that team, I would’ve fitted in perfectly.”

Well, Wayne, let us be the judge of that as we picture a world where Rooney does indeed join Pep Guardiola’s Barcelona team.

First, let’s discuss the kind of player he was.

Terrifyingly for the rest of us, there will be some football watchers who now know Rooney as a manager or a pundit more than they did as a player, so let us fill you in on what he was like on the pitch.

Simply put, Rooney was one of the best young talents ever seen in football. There were non-ridiculous comparisons between him, Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi.

Rooney never finished in the top three of the Ballon d’Or for his entire career, which seems mental to even think about, but if you would have asked anyone from 2005 to 2010, who the best player in the world was, he would have got a mention.

What made Rooney excellent was that he in a lot of ways a typical English striker. He is only 5ft 10’ so shorter than your average centre forward but what he lacked in going upwards, he made up for in going through.

Rooney weighed around 80kg during his United days. As a comparison, Eli Junior Kroupi is the same height and weighs 70kg. Yoane Wissa, also of a similar height, weighs 74kg.

But it was not fat that pushed Rooney up to the higher weight, it was muscle. Rio Ferdinand said Rooney had a “caveman” strength from a very young age. There are reports he was able to bench press 110 kg as a 15-year-old.

Rooney’s physicality was a nightmare for defenders to play against. We can all remember him for the reckless challenges and flying slide tackles but for every one of those, there are 20 examples of him muscling free of a defender.

A number nine who is strong isn’t groundbreaking but what separated Rooney from the pack was that he had the physicality but combined it with a technical ability rarely seen in an English centre forward.

It was his most continental ability and one that was there from very early on. Look at this goal for Everton against Arsenal, the one that had commentator Clive Tyldesley telling everyone to remember the name.

The experienced Sol Campbell gives Rooney plenty of space on the edge, for the logical reasons that this is a 16-year-old who does probably not have the confidence to be trying those kinds of shots and you would have to be a pretty good player to beat David Seaman from that range.

Given that space, Rooney looks up then picks his spot. He sidefoots it, giving it the curl needed to go up and down in the short space of time. Seaman is at full stretch and doesn’t get close to it. It kisses the bar on the way in one of the most perfectly hit shots in Premier League history.

There are countless examples of Rooney displaying the kind of technical superiority ahead of players in the league.

It was not just shooting too, Rooney was one of the best passers in the league too. His chip to Robin Van Persie in 2013 was hit hard enough to travel 40 yards in no time at all but with a delicacy that allowed it to slow and drop perfect for Van Persie, meaning the Dutchman did not have to break his stride before volleying it in.

Rooney’s ability was not lost on other players either. In 2015, he received this compliment from Xavi: “Wayne Rooney is a player I have admired for a long time. He is an extraordinary player with extraordinary capabilities.”

As well as the strength and technical ability Rooney had, he combined that with a relentlessness. Rooney grew up boxing in Merseyside, he is the footballing version of Rocky Balboa. And what that gave him was an incredible work rate. What he lacked in diet discipline over the summer, he made up in running hard yards during games, something he now laments the current United squad for failing to do.

That desire comes with a lot of positives, not least it gets the crowd on your side, but there are negatives too, such as being dragged out of position in search of the ball but also Rooney had a rawness and rashness when it came to challenges. Four club career red cards feels on the low side.

Put it all together and you have a physical, relentless player who also has the technique to play at the highest of levels. Now what about Barcelona?

The forgotten story of… Wayne Rooney’s Man Utd transfer request in 2010

The tactical philosophy of Pep Guardiola’s Barcelona has been well studied and adopted all over the world to varying degrees of success.

It was most effective at Barcelona due to being relatively in its infancy and also Guardiola was blessed with infinite talents who had been developed to play this exact style of football.

It resulted in two Champions Leagues, three league titles and the first ever sextuple. But what was it exactly?

The best example of it came in that Wembley final, when Barcelona picked apart Sir Alex Ferguson’s Manchester United.

Tiki-taka, as it came to be known, was an evolution on the foundations laid by Johan Cruyff. It can rather falsely be labelled as pass, pass, pass but every pass in a perfect Guardiola system is with a purpose. The idea is to pull your opponent into areas they don’t want to be so that their team becomes streched, opening gaps. Being a Barcelona player is as much about running off the ball to create space for your teammate as it is what you do on it.

For players to succeed in Pep’s system, they need the combination of great passing ability, the technical quality to quickly control the ball and release and the spatial awareness to create space for their teammates via their positioning. They also need to run an awful lot.

As for what Guardiola wanted from his number nine, he very rarely played with a traditional number nine. He tried it with Zlatan Ibrahimovic and it famously did not work, although they may just as much to do with his Swedish attitude as it is with his ability.

Typically though, Guardiola wanted a number nine who could drop deep and overload the midfield. Guardiola loves his teams to exploit the half spaces between defensive lines and by having a false nine, he could operate in the area too far forward for the centre backs and too deep for the midfielders.

So the profile of player we are looking for is a technically excellent, intelligent player who can operate just as well in a 10 as he can as a nine. And that sounds a lot like Wayne Rooney.

As Rooney showed in his late career once his speed gave way, he is able to drop deep and essentially play as an advanced midfielder. At Barcelona, his move to that position may have been expedited by Guardiola’s desire to have him play as a false nine.

Rooney’s physicality would also add something new to a largely unphysical Barcelona front line. At the time they had Messi, Pedro and David Villa, three players you would not describe as overly physical, even if Messi in particular is far stronger than he often gets credited for.

There is every reason to think that Rooney would actually work very well in a Barcelona system, the only issue is one that Ibrahimovic also ran into – Messi.

For that Wembley final, Guardiola deployed Messi in the number nine spot which is where he played for the majority of the season. It was a new tactic by Guardiola as in the previous season, Messi played 39 matches on the right side compared to 12 in the centre forward position.

In 2010/11, those numbers flipped with Messi playing 43 times through the middle compared to 11 on the wing. In those 43 games, Messi scored 46 goals.

In their ideal worlds, Messi and Rooney would likely have wanted to operate in similar areas of the pitch and there would only be one winner in a potential battle for supremacy.

So while Rooney would have worked in Guardiola’s Barcelona, he would have arguably been even more impactful in Luis Enrique’s Barcelona. By the time Enrique took over, Barcelona had become much more direct and played Luis Suarez as a typical nine who could bring both Messi and Neymar into play.

Put Rooney into that system and it would have been scary.

Overall, it is fair to say that a player as technically gifted as Rooney would have definitely worked at Barcelona but he would have found himself in the shadow of Messi as so many other great players did. Still, he probably would have had a lot of trophies to help him get over that fact.

#1478. The 10 most unfootballery footballers ever: Where does James Trafford rank in weird and wonderful list?

Manchester United, Arsenal, Chelsea, Everton and Leeds United have all employed footballers who you always felt somehow stumbled into the wrong profession.

We’re talking former NASA interns, qualified doctors and those with a keen interest in literary theory. Footballers aren’t supposed to be this interesting away from the pitch, but this lot have broken the mould in weird and wonderful ways.

Here are 10 of the least footballery footballers in history.

You remember him. The 6’3″ man mountain who went viral for looking more like a minor Game of Thrones character than a professional footballer.

With a club career away from the limelight in South Korea, Greece and his native Hungary, Euro 2024 catapulted the striker in front of a whole new audience.

“Of course, one or two get to me, I usually have a laugh about it,” he said about becoming a social media sensation.

“I was born this way, I have this body shape. I’m not saying that I was this big when I was born, but I have a basic physique. Genetics – I can’t change that.”

No shade here. In a sport increasingly populated by chiselled physiques and carefully curated Instagram accounts, it’s refreshing to see a full international who looks like he should be crushing skulls in Westeros. More of them, please.

After looking into Hungary's striker, Martin Adam, I discovered:

Ádám became the top goalscorer of the 2021–22 Nemzeti Bajnokság I season, netting 31 goals.

Scored his first goal for Hungary when he aged 28 years old. His goal securing Hungary qualification.

A bit landfill indie, a bit Mod revival. You can picture Baines in Paul Weller’s backing band, wearing a parka and looking mildly unimpressed on stage for two hours.

That’s not to say he was some great footballing eccentric, but Baines had a certain individuality that stood out a bit in the identikit culture of the Barclays era.

Back in Batty’s day, it wasn’t remotely unusual for England internationals and title-winning midfielders to look and sound like blokes you’d encounter at your local.

Media training wasn’t yet a finely tuned industry, sanding down every rough edge until footballers sounded like they’d been assembled on a production line of bland platitudes. Three points, take each game as it comes, you know the rest.

Batty wasn’t alone in that respect, but his almost total disappearance from public life since retiring is a pretty good indication of how little he ever cared for the circus.

Just look at his sensationally understated response to missing a vital penalty in England’s World Cup defeat to Argentina in 1998. You’d have thought he’d misplaced his car keys.

“You know what the position is before you step up and take a pen,” he said.

“I’m disappointed it didn’t work out right but I’m pleased I took one.”

Nevin isn’t the only footballer with a penchant for indie music, but his credentials go well beyond owning a few Smiths records.

He’s a brilliant broadcaster and his genuine enthusiasm for the game always shines through, but we still get the feeling that running down the wing for Chelsea and Everton denied him his true calling of playing keyboards for a Glaswegian dreampop band.

Once did a Peel session, supported the Cocteau Twins, reunited for a run of shows at 200-capacity venues back in 2016. He can but dream.

READ: All hail James Trafford: How the most normal bloke in elite football became England’s No.1

We can’t be certain, but we’re pretty sure that Hislop is the only 90s Premier League cult hero that could’ve worked for NASA. Let us reach out to Tony Yeboah and Georgi Kinkladze and get back to you.

“I had been attending university in the US on a football scholarship, and had been doing a summer internship at NASA the year before I graduated,” Hislop reminisced in an interview with FourFourTwo.

“After getting my degree in Mechanical Engineering, I was drafted by an indoor team called the Baltimore Blast. This was before the days of MLS. As it turned out, Baltimore were touring England that summer.

“We played Aston Villa in two indoor games. Dwight Yorke – another Trinidadian – had signed for them a couple of years previously.”

The Jacques Brel-inspired crooner album he released? The Ken Loach film he appeared in? Suddenly retiring at the age of 30 just because? Basically every word he’s ever uttered?

None of it at all footballery. We’re still not entirely convinced he was a real person. Some sort of post-rave collective fever dream apparition.

In a recent appearance on the Second Captains podcast, Bellerin delved into his admiration for Stefan Zweig, the Austrian literary giant known for his nuanced character studies and literary explorations of obsession, morality and the human psyche.

This guy used to line up alongside Andrea Pirlo and David Villa.

Never seen someone look less like a footballer pic.twitter.com/CQkp921ziW

Socrates was destined to be different from the very beginning. His father was a self-educated intellectual with a passion for philosophy and literature, and named his first three sons after figures from ancient Greece. His brothers were called Sostenes and Sofocles.

One formative childhood memory was watching his father dispose of his treasured library following Brazil’s 1964 military coup. He was 10 years old at the time.

As an adult, he became a qualified doctor, was an outspoken political activist and helped spearhead a revolutionary movement at Corinthians. He’d have been just as comfortable discussing Marxism over a bottle of red as he was dictating the tempo in midfield.

He smoked two packs of cigarettes a day, sported a magnificent beard, captained Brazil at two World Cups and briefly came out of retirement to rock up at Garforth Town.

Football has produced plenty of superstars, but precious few quite like Socrates. Almost certainly the coolest footballer in history.

#1474. The top goalscorers for club & country in 2026 so far: Kane, Yamal, Mbappe, Raphinha…

Big names from Real Madrid, Barcelona, Arsenal and Bayern Munich feature alongside some surprise names in the most prolific goalscorers of the calendar year so far.

Some big names are surprisingly absent from the most prolific goalscorers of 2026 to date.

Drawn from Europe’s five major leagues, here are the top 10 goalscorers in 2026 across club and international competitions.

Schick has had reason to celebrate in 2026. Earlier this year, he reached the milestone of 100 goals for Bayer Leverkusen.

He’s been on fire this season, with 12 goals from 14 games for the German side.

There won’t be any more international goals from Schick, though. He retired from Czech Republic duty after the World Cup.

The jury is still out on Gyokeres, who remains a perplexing forward.

This calendar year has seen him look borderline anonymous and increasingly sidelined at Arsenal.

And yet Gyokeres also fired Sweden to the World Cup with a hat-trick against Ukraine and a late winner against Poland. He’s basically the Ikea Gerd Muller at this point.

What a year it’s been for Malen. Started it as a benchwarmer at Aston Villa. Set to finish it as one of Europe’s most lethal strikers at Roma.

Malen made an immediate impact after his January move to the Italian capital and his scoring rate has barely slowed down since.

For some reason, his form hasn’t quite translated into international football; he hasn’t scored for the Netherlands at all this year.

But high-flying Roma are laughing. Malen almost won the Serie A golden boot last season despite arriving midway through and he’s a leading contender for the gong this season.

A surprise entry, perhaps, given his struggles for Real Madrid.

The Brazilian has scored just one La Liga goal so far this season, and his goalscoring has been downright ordinary for Los Blancos for quite some time now.

He’s scored 18 goals in all competitions for his club this calendar year, averaging out at a not-great average of one every 186 minutes. His Brazil team-mate Raphinha, by contrast, has averaged a goal every 70 minutes for Barcelona in 2026.

But his international exploits look considerably more impressive, while his five goals in this international break – two against Japan, a hat-trick against Singapore – come after five goals at the World Cup. He’s scored 11 goals in 14 appearances for the Selecao in 2026.

Vini’s place in Jose Mourinho’s favoured XI has come under threat from summer signing Yan Diomande. Going back to his club refreshed, with his confidence boosted, might just be what he needs.

A fairly recent entrant into the top 10 after heading into the international break on the back of a hat trick against Union Berlin.

Olise was the Bundesliga’s best assister last season but has been more than capable of finding the net himself a fair few times too.

He didn’t score any goals at the World Cup but netted the winner in Zinedine Zidane’s second game in charge of France. The best Fantasy Footballer around right now.

Yamal has long been talked up as a Ballon d’Or contender, and slowly but surely he’s getting the numbers to back it up.

The teenager’s goalscoring output has grown season on season, and 2025-26 was no exception. February’s hat-trick against Villarreal was evidence of a player about to go truly stratospheric.

Unfortunately, the final furlong of the campaign was hit by a hamstring injury, or else we suspect he’d be a few places higher up in this list.

He needed just 10 minutes in his first World Cup start to find the back of the net, although that would be his only goal in Spain’s triumph out in North America.

Now he’s looking fit and hungry – at least based on the evidence of his exceptional form of late.

The Brazilian has an exceptional tally of 33 goals for Barcelona so far this calendar year (plus one for Brazil), which is especially impressive when you consider he’s missed quite a lot of action due to injury.

He averages a goal every 49 minutes for Barca this season – to put that in context, Kylian Mbappe averages a goal every 84 minutes for Real Madrid.

Raphinha has scored in all but three of the Barca games he’s played in in 2026-27, scoring hat tricks in two, and currently leads the Europe-wide goalscoring charts with 15 in the league.

The top three are the last three winners of the European Golden Shoe. This list has taken a while to take shape, but the frontrunners are the usual suspects.

Haaland’s four goals against Iraq and Senegal in the group stages finally saw him climb up into the top 10, from which he was surprisingly absent in the latter half of the 2025-26 club season, before he added to his World Cup tally against the Ivory Coast. Then there were two goals against Brazil.

He finally drew a blank as Norway exited the World Cup at the hands of England at the quarter-final stage. He earned a well-deserved rest before spearheading Man City’s new era under Enzo Maresca.

Same as it ever was with nine goals in nine Premier League appearances for City this season, plus braces against Porto and PSG and another Champions League goal against his favourite opponents, RB Leipzig.

Like his rival Haaland, it somehow took Mbappe until mid-June to enter the top 10.

Mbappe kicked off the year in superb style, scoring in six successive starts for Real Madrid (nine goals in total) before dipping considerably with just one goal in his next seven appearances.

By the nature of his 10 goals at the World Cup, we don’t expect to see the Real Madrid superstar dropping back out. His Champions League record is pretty sensational.

Arguably the finest player in world football right now. How often have you been able to say that about an Englishman?

The only player in Europe’s five major leagues to average a better-than-goal-a-game output so far this calendar year, the England captain has 41 goals in 40 appearances for Bayern Munich in all competitions in 2026 – including home and away against Real Madrid and PSG.

He capped off his superb season with a hat-trick in the DFB Pokal final. Two goals against Croatia showed Kane carried his form into the World Cup, where he eventually scored six times.

Unbelievably, the Norway game was Kane’s first knockout appearance for club and country in 2025-26 in which he didn’t score. Which, of course, he followed with a blank against Argentina.

Surprisingly enough, Kane failed to add to his tally by drawing a blank in his first three Bayern appearances of the 2026-27 campaign.

But it’s back to normal service with his Bayern tally standing at 10 goals in 14 games. The Czechs and Croatia have been on the receiving end in the Nations League too.

Still some way to go before catching Lionel Messi’s calendar year record, mind.

#1473. SCOTLAND 2 NORTH MACEDONIA 1: John McGinn at the double to spare the blushes of Pocognoli's shaky Scots on skipper Robertson's big night

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:01 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 17:11 EST, 13 November 2026

On the night when the nation looked over its shoulder and celebrated the past, the here and now for Scotland looked distinctly uncertain.

Coming 40 years and a day after his friend, Sir Kenny Dalglish, pulled on a Scotland jersey for the 102nd and final time, Andy Robertson joined the great man on a mark which, for years, seemed beyond the reach of mere mortals.

By time up, history had mercifully repeated itself at Hampden. Back in the day, Dalglish, by then player-manager at Anfield, sailed into the international sunset on the back of a routine 3-0 win over Luxembourg.

Facing another opponent of modest ability, Robertson’s red letter day didn’t go quite as smoothly. Yet, when the Tottenham man is old and grey and reflecting on the night he created history, the annals will at least record a slender victory.

While his side did just about enough to prevail here, this was another fraught night for Sebastien Pocognoli.

You can talk about the need for patience under the new manager until the cows come home. But North Macedonia are 71st in FIFA’s rankings. Scotland are 43rd.

John McGinn celebrates in trademark fashion after netting Scotland's winner from the spot

At Hampden Park, in front of an expectant crowd, Scotland should be putting them to the sword with something to spare.

Yet, for long enough, the Belgian’s new-look side were flat, predictable and plodding. It said much that it took the intervention of VAR for them to get the penalty which would ultimately lead to three points being accrued.

John McGinn’s second half double saved the Belgian’s blushes and truthfully there was little else to get the Tartan Army off their seats.

Too many big-name players scarcely merited pass marks. Too few looked comfortable in the system the manager is trying to bed in.

If it was a step in the right direction, it was a small one. After five games under the affable Belgian, the progress has certainly not been startling.

While it goes without saying that beating the Swiss in St Gallen on Monday will be an inordinately tougher task, having some hope of moving up a place and securing a kinder draw for the Euros is still better than no hope.

Regardless of what pot they end up in when the draw is made in Belfast next month, a radical improvement will certainly be required across the board if they are to stand any chance of qualifying for the tournament via the front door.

As well as the achievements of Robertson and Dalglish, the career of Craig Gordon was acknowledged before the match with the 84-times capped keeper deservedly afforded a warm hand by the Tartan Army.

McGinn slots home his penalty after Ben Gannon-Doak had been brought down in the area

There were absolutely no excuses for Scotland here. North Macedonia were a tier-two team in name only. They arrived at Hampden having not won in 12 matches and not scored in eight.

Another Pocognoli game saw another back-three combination. This time Luke Graham was selected in the centre of the unit with Ryan Porteous and Kieran Tierney deployed either side of the Stoke man in what were their first appearances under the Belgian.

Robertson and Ben Gannon-Doak were tasked with providing the width in the 3-4-3. Scott McTominay slotted back into an advanced role beside John McGinn with the returning Che Adams asked to lead the line.

For all there was a healthy crowd in excess of 40,000 inside Hampden, the atmosphere was subdued. In the four Nations League games to date under the new manager, the side hadn’t exactly given the supporters much to feed off.

Despite some big guns returning, Scotland made a laboured start to their night’s work. It said much that Graham, on his second appearance, was busier than any defender in white.

The first opening came as a result of an opposition error. John McGinn found Billy Gilmour who fed the overlapping Robertson. The skipper’s cross was well out of Adams’ reach.

Sebastien Pocognoli got his first Hampden win as Scotland boss but it was a nervy night

Although Ljupche Doriev worried Angus Gunn with a curling effort, Scotland began to exert some degree of control on the match. Lewis Ferguson kept the visitors hemmed in with a header into McTominay’s feet. The Napoli man saw his shot on the spin well saved by Stole Dimitrievski.

Pocognoli was frustrated when Slovakian referee Michal Ocenas blew for a foul on McTominay, his justifiable gripe being that playing an advantage would have seen Robertson have a crack at goal.

Dimitrievski had a decent night. Although Adams’ flashing header from McGinn’s corner took a deflection, a reflex save at his near post added to Scotland’s frustration.

North Macedonia were a spirited but ordinary side. They still had enough to thwart Pocognoli’s men.

Gannon-Doak saw plenty of the ball down the right, yet the end product often wasn’t there. The Bournemouth man did tee up Billy Gilmour for one dangerous cross. McTominay tried to replicate his iconic overhead kick against Denmark nearly a year ago. This time, his aim wasn’t true.

You could hardly blame Pocognoli’s star man for failing to find the net on that occasion.

Scott McTominay attempts an overhead spectacular a year on from THAT goal at Hampden

That wasn’t the case a few moments later when Adams slipped him in. Dimitrievski saved McTominay’s strike with an outstretched leg when he should have been picking the ball out of his net.

Adams had just blazed a strike high over the top while one-on-one with the keeper although the offside flag saved his blushes.

The visitors came closer to edging ahead when Eljif Elmas played the pass of the match over Scotland’s static defence to pick out Ezgjan Alioski. His lay-off was smashed into the side net by Enis Bardhi.

A wholly uninspiring first-half concluded with Robertson advancing up the left and launching a cross halfway to Castlemilk. This was not going well.

Pocognoli waited on the edge of the pitch for his players returning, his enthusiastic applause clearly audible in the arena.

His hopes of a breakthrough at the outset of the second period were dashed in extraordinary fashion. Adams did well to chase a ball down to the line and cut it back. McTominay and his marker couldn’t connect, leaving Gilmour the simple task of firing into an unguarded net. Leaning back, his failure to even hit the target was unfathomable.

Elmin Rastoder celebrates after silencing Hampden with a leveller for North Macedonia

Within seconds, the sense of relief inside Hampden was palpable as the opener finally arrived. Porteous got enough distance on his clearing header for Adams to barge Visar Musliu out of the way.

McGinn was alert to the situation and burst into the box. His crisp strike finally had the beating of the goalkeeper.

It should have settled Pocognoli’s side and paved the way for a comfortable result. Instead, they were pegged back within three minutes.

It was all just so simple and so avoidable. Bardhi’s whipped corner only needed McTominay to outjump his man. Flat-footed as the delivery arrived, he could only watch on in horror as Elmin Rastoder’s flashing header beat Angus Gunn.

Although Gilmour worked the keeper with a low strike, North Macedonia also sniffed a second goal. Time and time again, they got into pockets of space on the flanks and fired in dangerous crosses.

Adams made way for Oli McBurnie, the Hull man desperately hoping for his first goal on his 21st international appearance. He had a gilt-edged chance to get off the mark when rolled in by McGinn, but selflessly passed to the overlapping Gannon-Doak.

Scotland move on to their final game away in Switzerland as they look to finish on a high note

The winger appeared to take a heavy touch which allowed the keeper to rescue the situation. VAR, however, spotted that Dimitrievski had impeded him. Penalty.

McGinn did the necessary from 12 yards, smashing the ball straight down the middle for his 24th international goal.

North Macedonia, to their credit, kept going for it. They sensed a fragility in Scotland. Everyone in the ground could.

McGinn’s calm conversion proved to be just about enough to get the job done. But it’s fair to suggest that we are still awaiting lift-off in the new era.

SCOTLAND (3-4-1-2): Gunn; Porteous, Graham, Tierney; Gannon-Doak (Hickey 76), Ferguson, Gilmour (Christie 76), Robertson; McGinn; Adams (McBurnie 67), McTominay. Booked: Ferguson. Manager: Sebastien Pocognoli.

NORTH MACEDONIA (4-2-3-1): Dimitrievski; Ilievski, Mladenovski, Musliu, Alioski; Gashtarov (Elezi 64), Elmas (Stankovski 78); Churlinov (Maleski 64), Bardhi, Doriev (Nikolov 85); Rastoder. Booked: None. Manager: Goce Sedloski.

#1472. The records that Max Dowman has already broken – & the next he could smash with Arsenal and England

Max Dowman is a little over a month away from his 17th birthday but he has already racked up an impressive number of records in football.

The Arsenal winger scored a late winner to give England U21s a 3-2 victory over France’s equivalent age group and in doing so, became the youngest scorer for England’s U21 age group.

That adds to a growing list of records the Arsenal man has already achieved.

Youngest goalscorer in Premier League history

While he missed out on the youngest player to feature in the Premier League by a couple of months to his Arsenal teammate Ethan Nwaneri, Dowman is currently the youngest goalscorer in Premier League history.

Dowman netted against Everton in March at the age of 16 years and 73 days, beating Everton’s James Vaughan to the record.

Vaughan scored back in April 2005 when he was 16 years and 270 days old. Other 16-year-olds to score in the top flight include James Milner, Wayne Rooney and Rio Ngumoha.

Youngest player to win the Premier League

Dowman already has a Premier League winners medal and is the youngest to have ever lifted the trophy.

Dowman was 16 years and 144 days when Arsenal lifted the trophy away at Crystal Palace on the final day of last season and took the record off Manchester City’s Phil Foden.

The first title Foden was involved in was the 2017/18 season when Foden was 17 years and 350 days old.

Dowman also had a bigger role than Foden as he played six, scored one and assisted one compared to Foden’s one assist in five games.

Manchester City’s Rico Lewis is third on the list having been 18 years and 188 days when City lifted the title in 2023.

Youngest player to appear in the UEFA Champions League

Dowman also has history in Europe too after he became the youngest player to ever feature in the Champions League.

He was 15 years, 10 months and four days when he appeared in Arsenal’s 3-0 win over Slavia Prague last year, beating the former record set by Dortmund’s Youssoufa Moukoko in 2020.

England Under-21s youngest-ever player and goalscorer

Dowman’s appearance in the 1-0 loss to Portugal earlier this month saw him become the youngest player to ever represent England at the U21 level, beating the previous record set by Jude Bellingham.

His goal against France added yet another record to his tally as he took another record away from Bellingham.

England’s next Ballon d’Or winner: Ranking the 5 favourites after Harry Kane’s historic triumph

With hopefully a long career ahead of him, there are plenty of records Dowman could break.

Dowman has two more chances to become the youngest Champions League winner in history. That record currently belongs to Nwankwo Kanu who was 18 years and 296 days old when Ajax won it in 1995.

Should Arsenal reach the final this season in Madrid, Dowman will be 17 years and 149 days old. Should Arsenal fail this year, Dowman could win it at the age of 18 years and 148 days the following season.

One record Dowman will not be able to achieve is becoming the youngest appearance maker in England history. This international break window was the final chance for Dowman to do it for he will be 17 years and 81 days by the time of the next one in March. Theo Walcott was 17 years and 75 days when he set the record back in 2006.

Given he started so young, Dowman has a good chance to break a lot of Arsenal records too.

The obvious one would be going after the record appearance holder. That currently belongs to David O’Leary who played 722 games from 1975 to 1993.

Dowman is just a tad short of that currently on 19 but say Arsenal play around 60 games a season and Dowman plays in every one of those, he would reach O’Leary in 12 seasons.

Obviously he is not going to play in every single match and so if we are a little more conservative, you could say he would reach that mark around 15/16 seasons from now, should he develop into a starter. 16 seasons from now would put him at 33 which is not over the hill for a footballer by any means.

If someone plays that amount of games, you would also fancy him to have a good chance of becoming Arsenal’s top scorer of all time. That accolade currently belongs to Thierry Henry who scored 228 in 377 games. Dowman is currently on three so plenty of ground to catch up.

Playing that many games will also likely see him come close to the top of the appearances makers in the Premier League. James Milner currently has that title, having played 658 games in the top division. Dowman is currently on eight.

#1471. Engineered bacteria are weaning farms away from synthetic fertilizers

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Mariana Lenharo is a reporter for Nature in New York City.

Scientists are engineering bacteria that can provide nitrogen, an essential ingredient for plant growth, to wheat crops. Credit: Shakeel Ahmed/Anadolu Agency/Getty

The world’s farms depend on synthetic nitrogen fertilizers to increase crop yields, but the production and use of these chemicals generates billions of tonnes of greenhouse-gas emissions every year. Now, scientists are making progress on a greener alternative: bioengineered bacteria.

This approach takes a cue from natural bacteria that ‘fix’ nitrogen into a useful form and provide it to certain plants. Scientists are engineering genetic features into bacteria with the aim of enabling them to fix nitrogen for important food crops, such as maize (corn) and wheat, that don’t have such natural microbial partners.

In a comment published on 10 November in Nature Biotechnology1, researchers suggest that bioengineered bacteria could eventually replace up to half of synthetic fertilizers. The bacteria deliver nitrogen more efficiently to roots than synthetic fertilizers do, which could reduce greenhouse-gas emissions and nitrogen pollution of waterways. But this would require a slew of advances, from getting different microbial species to work together to more-rigorous field trials.

How CRISPR could yield the next blockbuster cropSome of these ‘biofertilizers’ have been augmented with genes and genetic snippets from viruses or distantly related bacteria. This means that the engineered microbes are classified as transgenic — altered to include DNA from other species. The bacteria are now being trialled on small plots of maize on farms in the Midwestern United States. The bacteria, developed by Switch Bioworks in San Carlos, California, are the first example of a transgenic biofertilizer approved for testing on fields in the country.

How CRISPR could yield the next blockbuster crop

In September, Switch Bioworks received approval from the Brazilian regulatory agency, the National Technical Commission on Biosafety (CNTBio), to test its strains there. This is the first time that a transgenic bacterium of any kind has been approved for field tests in Brazil, says molecular biologist Mario Murakami, who is the president of CTNBio in Campinas.

Companies that have focused on editing bacterial genes rather than producing transgenic microbes are further along. Pivot Bio in Minneapolis, Minnesota, has applied its gene-edited biofertilizers to tens of millions of hectares of US farmland over the past decade, says the company’s chief technology officer Travis Frey. Some of Pivot Bio’s products have also been tested in Canada, Argentina, Kenya and Brazil.

Most plants can’t use the form of nitrogen that is present in the air. Some crops, including soya beans and peanuts, host colonies of bacteria that can convert atmospheric nitrogen into a usable form. The plant takes up that nitrogen and, in return, provides carbon that fuels bacterial growth. But most staple crops lack these microbial partners, leading farmers to rely on synthetic nitrogen fertilizers. These chemical fertilizers account for 5% of global greenhouse-gas emissions, and drive damaging nutrient pollution in waterways.

For decades, researchers have tried to get bacteria to fix nitrogen for staple crops. Until recently, the approach was to collect wild strains of nitrogen-fixing bacteria from soil and apply them to seeds or spray them onto plants. “It doesn’t work,” says Jean-Michel Ané, a bioengineer at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, who is working on microbial fertilizers. The wild microbes fail to thrive when applied to crops that don’t provide them with carbon.

How to climate-proof crops: scientists say the secret’s in the dirt

How to climate-proof crops: scientists say the secret’s in the dirt
